## The Water Flowing Down: Springs and Irrigation Channels Under Pressure

At six in the morning, before the thermometer has even begun its climb, the water in the Pampaneira irrigation channel flows with a murmur the farmers know by heart. Antonio García, ditch tender for the Pampaneira irrigation community, walks along the edge of the canal with a hoe on his shoulder and his eyes fixed on the flow. His job is to distribute a resource that no longer arrives in the abundance of the past: data from the community itself indicate that the summer flow has dropped by 25 percent since 1990. This figure, cold on paper, translates into shorter irrigation shifts and longer arguments among neighbors.

The irrigation channels of the Alpujarra, declared a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System by the FAO, form a hydraulic network of Andalusian origin that winds its way down impossible slopes. Their operation depends on a simple principle: the snowmelt from Sierra Nevada feeds the ravines, and the channels capture this water to carry it to the terraces and orchards. The problem is that the snowmelt has become unpredictable. It snows less, the snow melts earlier, and summers are growing longer, so the entire system is left without its main source of recharge just when it is needed most.

In Lanjarón, the town that has made water its hallmark, the springs show an equally worrying trend. Measurements by the Confederación Hidrográfica del Guadalquivir record an 18 percent drop in the flow of the springs that supply the municipality and its famous spa. Researcher Carmen Ruiz, a hydrologist at the Universidad de Granada, has been measuring these aquifers for a decade and sums up the situation with a phrase she repeats at conferences and neighborhood meetings: water does not disappear all at once, but rather retreats in silence. Her studies point to a combination of reduced snowfall and increased evapotranspiration, two phenomena that climate change is intensifying on the southern slopes of Sierra Nevada.

The paradox is that Lanjarón continues to sell its image as a town of water while the flows dwindle. The public fountains in the town center still flow, but with less force than three decades ago, and the older residents remember winters when there was enough water to waste. Today, management has become surgical: every liter is accounted for, every leak is hunted down, and every concession is scrutinized. The spa, the main economic driver of the municipality, has had to adapt its intakes and reduce consumption during periods of low water.

The irrigation channel system is not just a hydraulic infrastructure; it is also a social mechanism. Ditch tenders like Antonio García do not merely open and close gates: they mediate conflicts, know every plot of land and every owner, and apply customary law that has survived centuries of political change. The reduction in flow has strained this community fabric. At the assemblies of the irrigation community, voices are raised more frequently than before, and sanctions for exceeding irrigation limits are no longer a rarity.

The terraces of the Alpujarra, those green steps that trace the hillside, depend entirely on this gravity-fed irrigation. When water is scarce, tomato, pepper, and green bean crops suffer, and with them the subsistence economy still practiced by many families. Younger farmers have begun experimenting with drip irrigation systems fed by small reservoirs, but the rugged terrain complicates any modernization. Moreover, drip irrigation does not fulfill the same ecological function as the irrigation channels, which recharge aquifers and maintain soil moisture in a semi-arid landscape.

Scientists at the Universidad de Granada have documented another side effect: the loss of flow in the irrigation channels reduces the biodiversity associated with these wet corridors. Amphibians, aquatic insects, and birds that depend on the small ecosystems created by the irrigation water see their habitats shrink. The irrigation channel is not just a canal; it is an artificial river that sustains life as it flows. When it dries up, silence settles over the ravines.

In the upper basin of the Lanjarón river, sensors from the Confederación Hidrográfica del Guadalquivir record a trend that technicians describe as structural. It is not an isolated dry year, but a progressive decrease advancing in parallel with the rise in average temperatures in Sierra Nevada. Hydrological models project a further reduction in the flow available for irrigation in the coming decades, a scenario that forces a rethinking of the region's agricultural model. Some irrigation communities are already studying ways to reduce the cultivated area or prioritize crops with lower water demands.

The water flowing down from Sierra Nevada has shaped the Alpujarra for centuries. It has carved ravines, fed orchards, and sculpted a cultural landscape that now faces its greatest challenge. The irrigation channels are still there, tracing lines of life across the slopes, but the flow running through them is no longer what it once was. The data from Pampaneira and Lanjarón are not a local anecdote: they serve as a thermometer for a transformation affecting the entire southern slope of the peninsula. Meanwhile, the ditch tenders continue their morning rounds, hoes on their shoulders, distributing water that demands more effort and more negotiation every year.
